evidence.claim: An early auto-touring road crosses mountains and follows five rivers
evidence.quote: The Mohawk Trail opened in 1914 as one of the first auto-touring roads in the country. This 69-mile scenic byway meanders through deep forest and historic towns

evidence.claim: crosses mountains
evidence.quote: the highway descends steeply eastward from Whitcomb Summit down the slope of the Hoosac Range

evidence.claim: follows five rivers
evidence.quote: criss-crossing and paralleling five major rivers—the Millers, Connecticut, Green, Deerfield, and Hoosic.

evidence.claim: The Mohawk Trail climbs out of North Adams on a steep, curving road toward the Hoosac Range, then descends eastward beside the Cold River to the Deerfield.
evidence.quote: North Adams is the western terminus of the Mohawk Trail, which ascends to the West Summit along a steep, curving road.

evidence.claim: then descends eastward beside the Cold River to the Deerfield
evidence.quote: On the eastern side, the highway descends steeply eastward from Whitcomb Summit down the slope of the Hoosac Range following the Cold River to the Deerfield River.

evidence.claim: Forest, river crossings and historic towns define the 69-mile National Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: Mohawk Trail Scenic Byway National Scenic Byway • Massachusetts Length 69 mi / 111 km

evidence.claim: Forest, river crossings and historic towns
evidence.quote: This 69-mile scenic byway meanders through deep forest and historic towns

evidence.claim: Western Massachusetts Scenic Byways highlights its art museums, early tourist destinations and five rivers, from the Hoosic to the Millers.
evidence.quote: passing world-class art museums, early 20th-century tourist destinations, scenic hikes and dramatic vistas, all the while criss-crossing and paralleling five major rivers—the Millers, Connecticut, Green, Deerfield, and Hoosic.

evidence.claim: The corridor began as a Native American trading route across the Hoosac Range.
evidence.quote: The trail began as a Native American trade route which connected Atlantic tribes with tribes in Upstate New York and beyond. It followed the Millers River, Deerfield River and crossed the Hoosac Range

evidence.claim: European settlers later altered the route for horses and carts; growing automobile use brought another transformation.
evidence.quote: Later, the European settlers used the route, and eventually altered it, to support travel by horse and cart. As the use of automobiles increased, this route became the first to be constructed as a scenic auto touring route.

evidence.claim: The scenic road officially opened on October 22, 1914.
evidence.quote: The Mohawk Trail is the first scenic road in New England. It officially opened on October 22, 1914.

evidence.claim: Today’s Routes 2 and 2A follow much of the older trail. Along the Cold River, the historic footpath route lay north of the water; the modern road follows the south bank.
evidence.quote: Today the Mohawk Trail is a part of Routes 2 and 2A, following much of the original Indian trail.

evidence.claim: Along the Cold River, the historic footpath route lay north of the water; the modern road follows the south bank.
evidence.quote: This route, where the footpath itself is no longer extant in original form, is located on the north bank of the Cold River, with the modern roadway running along the south bank included in the listed area as an intrusion on the setting.

evidence.claim: River-powered mills helped these towns grow during the nineteenth century
evidence.quote: River-powered mills helped towns flourish all along the byway during the 19th century.

evidence.claim: the early auto route later brought souvenir shops, tourist cottages and restaurants
evidence.quote: Several Native American–themed souvenir shops, tourist cottages and restaurants from the era are still open today.

evidence.claim: Travel east from Williamstown through North Adams, climb past the hairpin turn to Whitcomb Summit, and descend toward Charlemont.
evidence.quote: passing through the communities of Orange, Erving, Gill, Greenfield, Shelburne, Buckland, Charlemont, Savoy, Florida, and North Adams.

evidence.claim: Travel east from Williamstown through North Adams
evidence.quote: from Athol, Massachusetts to the border with New York in Williamstown, Massachusetts, passing through the communities of Orange, Erving, Gill, Greenfield, Shelburne, Buckland, Charlemont, Savoy, Florida, and North Adams.

evidence.claim: climb past the hairpin turn to Whitcomb Summit, and descend toward Charlemont
evidence.quote: On the western side of the summit there is the popular hairpin turn and lookout, overlooking the city of North Adams and the Taconic Mountains. On the eastern side, the highway descends steeply eastward from Whitcomb Summit down the slope of the Hoosac Range following the Cold River to the Deerfield River.

evidence.claim: Follow the Deerfield toward Shelburne Falls and its former trolley bridge, now a flower garden.
evidence.quote: A portion of the trail parallels the Deerfield River for several miles, and passes through the village of Shelburne Falls, and the Bridge of Flowers.

evidence.claim: its former trolley bridge, now a flower garden
evidence.quote: The seasonal footbridge – once a trolley bridge – has a garden of flowers covering it.

evidence.claim: Beyond Greenfield, the French King Bridge crosses the Connecticut; farther east the Millers River accompanies the route through Erving toward Orange and Athol.
evidence.quote: Millers River runs near the entire eastern section of the byway, and parallels it through the town of Erving. In Gill, the French King Bridge rises high above the Connecticut River.

evidence.claim: toward Orange and Athol
evidence.quote: The trail is generally considered to follow Route 2A in the east (which diverges from Route 2 as it goes through the town centers of Athol, Orange, and Greenfield)

evidence.claim: On the western side of Whitcomb Summit, the hairpin turn’s lookout faces North Adams and the Taconic Mountains.
evidence.quote: On the western side of the summit there is the popular hairpin turn and lookout, overlooking the city of North Adams and the Taconic Mountains.

evidence.claim: The road climbs steeply from the city toward the West Summit.
evidence.quote: North Adams is the western terminus of the Mohawk Trail, which ascends to the West Summit along a steep, curving road.

evidence.claim: North Adams occupies the Hoosic River valley, where the meeting of two river branches supplied water power for early manufacturing.
evidence.quote: Manufacturing began in the city before the Revolutionary War, largely because the confluence of the Hoosic River's two branches provided water power for small-scale industry.

evidence.claim: North Adams occupies the Hoosic River valley
evidence.quote: North Adams is located in the valley created by the Hoosic River

evidence.claim: Farther east, the mountain crossing takes a different line: from Whitcomb Summit, the highway descends the Hoosac Range along the Cold River to the Deerfield.
evidence.quote: On the eastern side, the highway descends steeply eastward from Whitcomb Summit down the slope of the Hoosac Range following the Cold River to the Deerfield River.

evidence.claim: The scenic road opened in 1914, among the country’s early routes built for auto touring through this landscape.
evidence.quote: The Mohawk Trail opened in 1914 as one of the first auto-touring roads in the country.

evidence.claim: North Adams and the Taconic Mountains are visible from the hairpin lookout.
evidence.quote: lookout, overlooking the city of North Adams and the Taconic Mountains.

evidence.claim: A water main helped save the trolley bridge that became Shelburne Falls’ flower garden.
evidence.quote: Since it was not needed as a footbridge and could not be demolished because it carried a water main between the two towns, the community agreed to her idea.

evidence.claim: The garden occupies a seasonal footbridge connecting Shelburne and Buckland.
evidence.quote: The Bridge of Flowers is in Shelburne Falls, Massachusetts, connecting the towns of Shelburne and Buckland. The seasonal footbridge – once a trolley bridge – has a garden of flowers covering it.

evidence.claim: Built in 1908 for the Shelburne Falls and Colrain Street Railway, it connected rail freight with Colrain. The neighboring Iron Bridge had a twenty-ton weight limit.
evidence.quote: Built for $20,000 in 1908 by the Shelburne Falls and Colrain Street Railway, so that freight could be picked up and dropped off directly from the railroads and brought to Colrain. This concrete bridge was necessary because the nearby Iron Bridge had a twenty-ton weight limit.

evidence.claim: As trucks gained freight business, the railway went bankrupt in 1927.
evidence.quote: As automobile usage began to increase, freight began to be transported more by trucks, and the street railway (trolley) company went bankrupt in 1927.

evidence.claim: Antoinette Burnham proposed a garden, and local women’s clubs raised money for the transformation.
evidence.quote: Antoinette Burnham came up with the idea of transforming the bridge into a garden.

evidence.claim: local women’s clubs raised money for the transformation
evidence.quote: Several women's clubs around town raised $1,000 in 1929.

evidence.claim: Eighty loads of loam arrived in 1929. Beneath the flowers, soil reaches two and a half feet deep over the arches and nine feet at the piers.
evidence.quote: In 1929, eighty loads of loam and several loads of fertilizer were brought to the bridge.

evidence.claim: soil reaches two and a half feet deep over the arches and nine feet at the piers
evidence.quote: The bridge contains two and a half feet of soil at the top of the arches and nine feet deep at the piers.

evidence.claim: The French King Bridge carries Route 2 across the Connecticut River between Gill and Erving.
evidence.quote: The French King Bridge is the three-span "cantilever arch" bridge that crosses the Connecticut River on the border between the towns of Erving and Gill, Massachusetts, United States.

evidence.claim: carries Route 2
evidence.quote: The bridge, part of Massachusetts Route 2, carries automobile, bicycle, and pedestrian traffic

evidence.claim: Its opening in 1932 changed the highway’s course: Route 2 moved from the older crossing through Turners Falls to French King Highway.
evidence.quote: In 1932, a more modern bridge capable of handling the increased automobile traffic, the French King Bridge, opened further upstream and Route 2 was relocated to its modern alignment along French King Highway.

evidence.claim: The American Institute of Steel Construction awarded it the title “Most Beautiful Steel Bridge” for 1932, the year it opened to traffic.
evidence.quote: It was named the "Most Beautiful Steel Bridge" of 1932 by the American Institute of Steel Construction.

evidence.claim: The bridge was rebuilt in 1992 and refurbished in 2008–2010.
evidence.quote: The bridge was rebuilt in 1992, and refurbished in 2008–2010.

evidence.claim: Nine-foot steel barriers were added on both sides in 2023.
evidence.quote: In 2023, a nine-foot high steel barrier was erected on both sides of the bridge by the MassDOT.

evidence.claim: Its name comes from French King Rock, visible in the middle of the river.
evidence.quote: The name comes from a nearby geographical feature named French King Rock, visible in the middle of the river.

Whitcomb Summit elevation differs between cached Wikipedia pages (2,272 and 2,172 feet); omit the current draft’s elevation.

Bridge of Flowers cache dates the garden proposal to 1929 but club sponsorship to 1928. Omit proposal year. Wikipedia reports reopening in 2025, but no site-manager page is cached to verify present access; do not promise access or operating dates.

No Indigenous community source is cached for the trail’s early history; omit precise antiquity and generalized claims about individual nations. Cached spellings Pocumtuck, Pocumtuk and Pocomtuc differ across town pages.
